analysis.one_liner: Terminates annual direct subsidy payments to farm operations and caps other farm payment limits.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Agriculture Committee and its subcommittee, and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 112th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would end the direct payments program, which sends a set annual check to owners of certain crop land regardless of prices or production, starting with the 2012 crop year. It would also set a single hard cap of $65,000 per person per crop year on the remaining counter-cyclical and ACRE revenue payments. Direct payments cost roughly $5 billion a year and were widely criticized for flowing disproportionately to large farm operations and landowners rather than small family farms.
analysis.who_benefits: Federal taxpayers, who would save the roughly $5 billion a year the direct payments program costs, since the payments go out whether prices are high or low and concentrate among the largest commodity producers.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the direct payments program for covered commodities and peanuts for the 2012 crop year, ending automatic annual checks unrelated to crop prices or yields [S2] [S3].
Caps counter-cyclical and ACRE payments at $65,000 per person per crop year, tightening the payment limit so the largest recipients cannot stack multiple program payments [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Owners and operators of farm land enrolled in the direct payments program, chiefly large commodity grain and peanut operations, along with the largest recipients of counter-cyclical and ACRE payments who would face the new $65,000 cap.

drawbacks.text: Farmers receiving direct payments would lose a guaranteed annual income stream they had planned around, and some would argue the payments were promised in exchange for earlier reforms that cut their support in the 1996 and 2002 farm bills; abrupt termination in a single crop year gives recipients no transition period [S2] [S3].

Rural economies in heavily subsidized commodity regions could see reduced spending if payments end without a phase-out, an objection farm-state members of both parties commonly raised to ending direct payments.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is roughly $5 billion a year in deficit savings against the loss of a guaranteed payment stream for commodity farmers, concentrated among the largest operations. The single-crop-year effective date with no transition is the weakest design feature; a phase-out would have softened the blow to individual farmers. On balance the bill targets a program that paid out regardless of need or market conditions, and its payment cap addresses stacking of subsidies by the largest recipients.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Agriculture Committee and its General Farm Commodities subcommittee on the day it was introduced, and it sat there with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote for the rest of the 112th Congress.

narrative.text: Rep. Jeff Flake introduced the bill on July 11, 2011, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Agriculture [S1] [S5].
On July 22, 2011, it was referred to the Subcommittee on General Farm Commodities and Risk Management, where it remained for the rest of the Congress [S5].
The bill attracted 18 cosponsors, 13 Democrats and 5 Republicans, but the Agriculture Committee took no further action and no version ever reached the House floor [S4] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Recipients of direct farm payments, especially large commodity operations, kept their guaranteed annual payments because the bill never advanced; taxpayers gained nothing from the bill's defeat.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Direct payment recipients, chiefly large farms

for.name: Rep. Jeff Flake
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to terminate direct payments and tighten payment limits, and recruited 18 cosponsors.

for.name: 13 of 435 House members (Democrats) and 5 Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, making it a bipartisan effort across both parties.

against.name: House Agriculture Committee leadership
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction, chaired by Rep. Frank Lucas (R-OK)
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to a subcommittee and never scheduled a hearing or markup, leaving it without a path to the floor.

against.name: Commodity farm organizations and large subsidized farm operations
against.what_they_did: Opposed terminating direct payments during the run-up to the 2012 farm bill, pressing the Agriculture Committee to preserve the program.

sides.party_line_note: The 18 cosponsors split 13 Democrats to 5 Republicans, but the bill died in committee without a vote, so no floor vote ever revealed how the full chamber would divide.

industries.industry: Large commodity grain and peanut operations
industries.note: Direct payments were automatic annual checks based on historical crop acreage, not need, so the largest enrolled operations received the biggest checks; termination would cost them billions. The industry's interest in keeping the payments ran against taxpayers, who bore the cost.

Ending direct payments for the 2012 crop year would have saved roughly $5 billion a year, the program's annual cost, and the $65,000 cap would have limited further outlays on counter-cyclical and ACRE payments.
